Three HTTP versions carry the same three files.

Watch what one lost packet does in each version.

Methods, status codes and headers mean the same in every version.

Only the framing and the transport change.

On one HTTP/1.1 connection, the browser sends GET A,

waits for response A, and only then sends GET B.

If response A is slow, B and C wait behind it.

So browsers open several TCP connections per host instead.

HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames.

Frames of streams A, B and C interleave on one TCP connection.

A TCP packet with a frame of A is lost.

TCP delivers bytes only in order,

so frames of B and C wait too.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP.

Each request gets its own QUIC stream:

A on stream 0, B on 4, C on 8.

On HTTP/3 over QUIC,

the same lost packet delays only stream 0, response A.

On HTTP/2 over TCP, all three waited.

During the TLS handshake, the client offers protocol names with ALPN,

such as h2 and http/1.1.

The server picks one.

A server advertises h3 with the Alt-Svc header.

The client opens QUIC with ALPN h3,

and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.
